rashi:a1.1: Mishna: All these are karet transgressions when committed intentionally without a warning. But if there was a warning, some of them are punished by strangulation, some by stoning and some by lashes; and when committed unwittingly, by a sin offering. And as for why the mishna began by teaching the forbidden relations of a mother and a father’s wife and so on, then broke off and taught in between one who has intercourse with a male or with an animal and a woman who brings an animal upon her, and then began again to teach a woman and her daughter, and did not teach them all together in the first group: it is because we have established in Sanhedrin (53a) that all those it listed first, a mother, a father’s wife, a daughter-in-law, and one who has intercourse with a male or with an animal, are punished by stoning. That is why it taught them first, since [stoning] is more severe than the other death penalties of the court.
rashi:a1.2: A woman and her daughter: her daughter’s daughter and her son’s daughter are included; and likewise his own daughter, his daughter’s daughter and his son’s daughter, his mother-in-law, his mother-in-law’s mother and his father-in-law’s mother are included in this.
rashi:a2.1: One who blasphemes: there is one who says (Sanhedrin 56) it is one who “blesses” the Name [a euphemism for cursing it], and there is one who says it is one who chants and sings to an idol.
rashi:a2.2: The karet for notar is explained later in this chapter (Keritot 5a): “And whoever eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned the sacred thing of the Lord, and that soul shall be cut off” (Leviticus 19:8); and below we establish that verse as speaking of notar.
rashi:a2.3: And the karet for piggul is also explained later in the chapter (there): it is derived from notar through the shared word “iniquity.” For of piggul it is written: “And if any of the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings is eaten on the third day, it shall not be accepted, neither shall it be credited to the one who offers it; it shall be piggul, and the soul that eats of it shall bear its iniquity” (Leviticus 7:18); and of notar it is written: “And whoever eats it shall bear his iniquity.” Just as there, with notar, where “iniquity” is written, the punishment is karet, so too with piggul, where “shall bear its iniquity” is written, it is karet.
rashi:a2.4: One who slaughters consecrated animals outside is liable to karet even if he did not offer them up, as it is written: “And has not brought it to the door of the Tent of Meeting … blood shall be imputed to that man; he has shed blood, and that man shall be cut off” (Leviticus 17:4). And one who offers up outside is also liable to karet, as it is written: “Who offers up a burnt offering or sacrifice, and does not bring it to the door of the Tent of Meeting …” (Leviticus 17:8–9). And if he unwittingly slaughtered and unwittingly offered up, he is liable to two sin offerings.
rashi:a3.1:
And the Paschal offering and circumcision are positive mitzvot, and carry karet. The Paschal offering carries karet, as it is written: “But the man who is pure …” (Numbers 9:13). Circumcision carries karet, as it is written: “And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised … that soul shall be cut off” (Genesis 17:14). These two, the Paschal offering and circumcision, are positive mitzvot [and there is no offering for their unwitting violation], but all the others are prohibitions and carry an offering, since an offering comes only for a prohibition, as is explained below.

For example, the prohibitions of the forbidden relations are stated explicitly. For the blasphemer we find a prohibition, “You shall not curse God” (Exodus 22:27), and karet too, as it is written: “But the soul that acts high-handedly … he blasphemes the Lord, and that soul shall be cut off” (Numbers 15:30). For all the forbidden relations above, karet is written, since the conclusion includes them all: “The souls that do them shall be cut off” (Leviticus 18:29); and a prohibition is written for every one of them, “The nakedness of your mother you shall not uncover” (Leviticus 18:7), and for all of them “you shall not uncover” is written. For a menstruating woman too there is a prohibition, “And you shall not approach a woman in the impurity of her menstruation” (Leviticus 18:19), and the karet for a menstruating woman is included with the others, since after all the forbidden relations it is written: “The souls that do them shall be cut off.” And the reason karet is not written for the wife of his mother’s brother, nor for his mother-in-law’s mother’s mother, is that they are secondary relations forbidden by the Sages and not written in the Torah.

One who worships an idol also has a prohibition and karet: the prohibition, as it is written, “For you shall bow down to no other god” (Exodus 34:14); and karet, as it is written, “Because he has despised the word of the Lord and has broken His commandment, that soul shall be utterly cut off” (Numbers 15:31). That verse speaks of idol worship, for [the idolater] has despised the word of the Lord, as the Master said in Sanhedrin (99a): “I am” and “You shall have no [other gods]” we heard from the mouth of the Almighty, and “You shall have no” speaks of idol worship. The prohibition of Molekh: “And you shall not give any of your seed to pass to Molekh” (Leviticus 18:21), or alternatively, “There shall not be found among you anyone who passes his son or his daughter through the fire” (Deuteronomy 18:10). There is karet as well, as it is written: “Any man of the children of Israel … who gives of his seed to Molekh shall be put to death” (Leviticus 20:2), and after it: “I will set My face against that man and will cut him off” (Leviticus 20:3). The necromancer also has a warning, as it is written, “Do not turn to the ghosts …” (Leviticus 19:31), and karet, as it is written, “And the soul that turns to the ghosts …” (Leviticus 20:6); the Gemara explains why the mishna does not list the yidde’oni here. One who desecrates Shabbat has a warning, “You shall not do any labor” (Exodus 20:10), and karet, “For whoever does any labor on it, that soul shall be cut off” (Exodus 31:14). An impure person who ate sacred food: a prohibition, “He shall not eat [of the sacred things] until he is pure” (Leviticus 22:4), and karet, “Say to them: Throughout your generations, any man who approaches … with his impurity upon him, that soul shall be cut off” (Leviticus 22:3). One who enters the Temple impure: the prohibition, “And she shall not come into the Sanctuary” (Leviticus 12:4), and “that they not defile their camps” (Numbers 5:3); karet, “He has defiled the Tabernacle of the Lord, and that soul shall be cut off” (Numbers 19:13). Eating fat and blood: a prohibition, “You shall eat neither fat nor blood” (Leviticus 3:17); karet for fat, “For whoever eats the fat … that soul shall be cut off” (Leviticus 7:25); karet for blood, “For the life of all flesh is its blood … whoever eats it shall be cut off” (Leviticus 17:14). The warning for notar: “And you shall burn the leftover in fire; it shall not be eaten” (Exodus 29:34); karet, as we said: “And whoever eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned the sacred thing of the Lord, and that soul shall be cut off.” The warning for piggul we derive from this verse: “And if any of the flesh … is left … it shall not be eaten, because it is sacred,” as we learn in the second chapter of Pesachim (24a): “It shall not be eaten, because it is sacred”: anything disqualified among sacred things, the verse comes to give a prohibition against eating it; and karet, as we said, is derived from notar through the shared word “iniquity.”

One who slaughters outside is explained in this chapter (3b): it is a prohibition according to the one who derives it by verbal analogy: “bringing” is written with offering up, “and does not bring it to the door of the Tent of Meeting,” and “bringing” is stated here with slaughter, “and has not brought it to the door of the Tent of Meeting”; just as there the Torah did not punish without first warning, so too here it did not punish without first warning. And according to the one who derives it by juxtaposition, the verse states: “There you shall offer your burnt offerings and there you shall do” (Deuteronomy 12:14): just as for offering up the Torah did not punish without first warning, so too for slaughter. One who offers up outside: the prohibition, “Take heed lest you offer up …” (Deuteronomy 12:13), and wherever it says “take heed,” “lest” or “do not,” it is a prohibition; and karet, as we said above: “Who offers up a burnt offering or a sacrifice ….” One who eats leavened bread: the prohibition, “You shall eat nothing leavened” (Exodus 12:20); karet, “For whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall be cut off” (Exodus 12:15).

One who eats on Yom Kippur: the prohibition is explained in Yoma (81a): “For whatever soul it is that is not afflicted” (Leviticus 23:29), and it derives “affliction” from “affliction” there: “because he has afflicted his neighbor’s wife” (Deuteronomy 22:24); just as there the Torah did not punish without first warning, so too here. And one who eats also incurs karet, as it is written of eating on Yom Kippur: “For whatever soul it is that is not afflicted … shall be cut off” (Leviticus 23:29). This “not afflicted” speaks of the affliction of eating, since it derives (Yoma 74b) “affliction” from “affliction” there, as it is written: “And He afflicted you and let you hunger” (Deuteronomy 8:3); just as there the affliction is hunger, so too here the affliction is hunger. One who performs labor on Yom Kippur has a warning: “And you shall do no manner of labor on that very day” (Leviticus 23:28); karet, as it is written: “I will destroy [that soul]” (Leviticus 23:30), and that is karet.

One who blends the oil: the prohibition, “Neither shall you make any like it according to its composition” (Exodus 30:32); karet, “Whoever compounds any like it … shall be cut off” (Exodus 30:33). And one who blends the incense: for his own use, to smell it. One who blends the oil [in the manner Moses made it in the wilderness, as it is written]: “Take you also the chief spices” (Exodus 30:23). One who blends the incense [mixing the eleven spices of the incense, as it is written]: “Take you sweet spices, balsam and onycha and galbanum” (Exodus 30:34). One who applies the anointing oil also has a prohibition, “Upon the flesh of man it shall not be applied” (Exodus 30:32), and karet, “Or whoever puts any of it upon a stranger shall be cut off from his people” (Exodus 30:33): [this means] of the anointing oil that Moses made. One who blends the incense: the warning, “According to its composition you shall not make for yourselves” (Exodus 30:37); karet, “Whoever shall make like it, to smell it, shall be cut off” (Exodus 30:38). But one who smells the incense of the Temple has neither a warning nor karet, since smell is not subject to misuse of consecrated property. It is unlike applying the anointing oil, which involves an act; therefore that carries a prohibition and karet.
rashi:a3.2: The Paschal offering and circumcision are positive mitzvot: the Paschal offering, as it is written, “And you shall sacrifice the Passover offering” (Deuteronomy 16:2); and circumcision, “And on the eighth day [the flesh of his foreskin] shall be circumcised” (Leviticus 12:3); and they carry karet, as we said. Among these are some liable to a death penalty of the court, such as one who worships an idol and one who desecrates Shabbat, and even so they are liable to karet when committed intentionally without a warning. If he was warned, some are punished by strangulation and some by stoning, as we said at the start. If he was not warned, he has escaped the court’s death penalty but he has not escaped karet; and karet is that he dies without children.
rashi:a4.1: For its unwitting violation, a sin offering: this is derived from idol worship, of which it is written, “And when you err and do not observe all these commandments” (Numbers 15:22); and the Master said (Horayot 8a): Idol worship is equal to the whole Torah, since “commandments” is written of it. And an offering is written of it: “Then he shall bring a she-goat in its first year” (Numbers 15:27). We derive: just as idol worship is something for whose intentional violation one is liable to karet and for whose unwitting violation one is liable to a sin offering, so too anything for whose intentional violation one is liable to karet, one is liable to a sin offering for its unwitting violation, such as these karet transgressions. The unwitting violation of the forbidden relations: he thought she was his wife. And one who has intercourse with a male or with an animal unwittingly: he thought to have intercourse with his wife in an unnatural manner, and had intercourse with a male or with an animal, and afterward it became known to him that it was a male or an animal; he brings a sin offering.
rashi:a4.2: And for their “unknown,” a provisional guilt offering: where he does not know whether he had intercourse with his wife in an unnatural manner, or with a male or an animal; and the same applies to the others. The woman who brings an animal upon her: she thought she was bringing a person, and it was an animal. A menstruating woman: he thought she was pure. The blasphemer: he thought he was “blessing” a two-letter name, and “blessed” the four-letter name, since one is liable only for the four-letter name, as we say in the fourth chapter [of Sanhedrin], on the death penalties (Sanhedrin 56a). Idol worship: he thought the Torah forbade sacrificing and burning incense but not bowing and pouring libations, for these four are all modes of worship. Molekh: he thought to pass another person through, and passed his own son. The necromancer: he intended a different kind of sorcery. Shabbat: he thought it was a weekday. Sacred food: he thought it was non-sacred meat. The Temple: he thought it was another building. Fat: he thought it was permitted fat. And blood: he thought it was spleen; another version: blood, he thought it was the blood of locusts or of fish; this is my teacher’s wording. Notar and piggul: he thought it was fit. One who slaughters outside: he thought it was a non-sacred animal. One who offers up: after private altars were forbidden, he sacrificed on such an altar, thinking that these altars, the public ones, were permitted; and the verse is established as referring to a private altar. Passover and Yom Kippur: he thought they were weekdays. The oil and the incense: he intended other spices, and they turned out to be the spices written [in the Torah]. But one who says it is entirely permitted, uprooting the whole prohibition, is not acting unwittingly but under duress, and is exempt.
rashi:a4.3: Unknown: his wife and his sister were in the bed; he thought he was having intercourse with his wife, and he does not know with which of them he had intercourse.
rashi:a4.4: Because he is [liable to] a sliding-scale offering: and a provisional guilt offering comes only for an uncertainty about a fixed [sin offering], as we say in the last chapter (below, Keritot 25a): A provisional guilt offering comes only for something whose intentional violation is punishable by karet and whose unwitting violation requires a fixed sin offering.
rashi:a5.1: Even the blasphemer: the Gemara explains what this means.
tosafot:a1.1: Mishna, thirty-six karet transgressions: first it teaches the forbidden relations punished by stoning, as Rashi explained; then it teaches a woman and her daughter, which is punished by burning; and then it teaches a married woman, punished by strangulation. That is why it did not interrupt them with the other transgressions punished by stoning.
gershom:a1.1: There are thirty-six karet transgressions in the Torah, for whose intentional violation one is liable to karet and for whose unwitting violation one is liable to a sin offering. Some of them carry a death penalty of the court when there are witnesses and a warning; if there are no witnesses and no warning, their intentional violation is punished by karet.
gershom:a2.1: One who has intercourse with a mother and so on; one who has intercourse with a male and so on: it goes back and teaches one who has intercourse with a male because these are a different kind of prohibition; and all of these are stoned when there are witnesses and a warning.
gershom:a3.1: One who has intercourse with a woman and so on: some of them carry a death penalty of the court, and some carry karet alone. (A printer’s gloss: this needs examination, since one who has intercourse with his sister, his father’s sister and so on, up to one who has intercourse with a menstruating woman, none of these carries a death penalty of the court at all. Perhaps the text is corrupt and should read: for example, one who has intercourse with his sister onward, up to and including one who has intercourse with a menstruating woman.) For example, one who has intercourse with a menstruating woman, and an impure person who ate sacred food, and so on.
gershom:a4.1: For these: the thirty-six, one is liable to karet for their intentional violation, to a sin offering for their unwitting violation, and [to a provisional guilt offering] for their “unknown”: for example, where forbidden fat and permitted fat were before him and he does not know which of them he ate.
rashi:b3.1: Lacking atonement: they may not eat sacrificial food until they bring their atonement offering; they are explained in chapter 2 (below, Keritot 8b).
rashi:b4.1: Until the blood is sprinkled: as is explained in chapter 2 (there, 9a): “As you are, so shall the stranger be” (Numbers 15:15): just as your ancestors entered the covenant only through circumcision, immersion and the sprinkling of blood, and so on.
rashi:b4.2: That is why it teaches four: wherever a mishna teaches a tally, it teaches it precisely; do not say it taught some cases and left others out.
rashi:b5.1: Four bring an offering for the intentional: explained in chapter 2 (there).
rashi:b8.1: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda: who says so below (there, 9b).
rashi:b8.2: The naziriteship of purity: a nazirite who became impure and counted seven days, so as to go back and begin counting a naziriteship of purity: it takes effect from the seventh. Then you find that he brings one offering for many impurities, for example where he became impure on the seventh and again on the seventh. Since he is pure on the seventh, these are three impurities, and there is one offering and not one for each impurity, because in the first two impurities he never reached a time fit for bringing an offering, since the offering is brought only on the eighth. Therefore he brings an offering only for the last. That is why it says “became impure on the seventh” twice: it refers to three impurities, since the mishna teaches “many impurities.”
rashi:b10.1: One long impurity: since he never came to a state of purity.
rashi:b11.1: Rather, conclude from it, and so on: that is why it teaches the tally, to tell us that it is precise; do not say it is Rabbi’s view and delete the nazirite from here.
rashi:b12.1: And he shall sanctify his head: for the second naziriteship, the naziriteship of purity.
rashi:b13.1: Five bring a sliding-scale offering: that is, for five transgressions one brings a sliding-scale offering, in chapter 2 (there).
rashi:b13.2: Why do I need the tally? Let it teach: “These [bring] ….”
rashi:b14.1: Because it teaches in the latter clause: in Horayot, chapter 2 (8b), which deals with these five and teaches as follows: The court is not liable for the hearing of the voice, or for the utterance of the lips, and so on; and a king is like them, also exempt for these, since a sliding-scale offering does not apply to him, for poverty is not common in a king. Rabbi Eliezer says: A king brings a goat, as is his law for all the mitzvot in the Torah. And we say in the Gemara there that Rabbi Eliezer said this only of defiling the Temple and its sacred foods, since karet is stated of them as with [transgressions requiring] a fixed offering. That is why it teaches five here, to tell us that it is precise: everyone who brings an offering for these five transgressions brings not a fixed offering but a sliding-scale one. Do not say: delete defiling the Temple and its sacred foods from here, to establish the mishna according to Rabbi Eliezer, who says a king brings a fixed offering for it. Rather, he does not bring a fixed offering: either according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who exempts him entirely, or according to Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Shimon, who obligate him in a sliding-scale offering, that is, a lamb or a she-goat, or turtledoves and young pigeons.
rashi:b16.1: Thirteen and twenty-four: they are explained there, in the chapter “Four Primary Categories of Damage” (Bava Kamma 4b), and also [which of them pay] from the best [land], as is explained there.
rashi:b16.2: An informer [masor]: one who denounces [another to the authorities].
rashi:b16.3: And one who renders piggul: a priest who rendered a Jew’s offering piggul by intending to eat it beyond its time. Though he is liable, he does not pay from the best [land], since this damage is mere speech and is damage that is not discernible.
rashi:b19.1: His sister: she was included among the forbidden relations, of which it is written, “The souls that do them shall be cut off” (Leviticus 18:29); and then in the portion of Kedoshim it is written again: “And if a man shall take his sister … they shall be cut off in the sight of the children of their people” (Leviticus 20:17).
rashi:b20.1: His sister, whom the verse detailed: when he commits it together with the others, he should be liable one offering for her, and one for all the others together. And if you ask: we have found that his sister was singled out to separate, but why were the other forbidden relations singled out [again in Leviticus 20]? The answer is: to teach us that they carry a death penalty of the court. The relations singled out there are those of which “shall surely be put to death” is written [some by stoning and some by strangulation], and some of which burning is written. And those there that carry karet, why the verse detailed them is explained in Yevamot (54a); but his sister, which is the one needed here, is not explained there.
rashi:b22.1: In the general category of all sacrificial offerings: “Say to them: Throughout your generations, any man of all your seed who approaches the sacred things …” (Leviticus 22:3). One cannot say that this “approaches” means actual touching, since touching does not carry the taking of life [karet], as we read in tractate Makkot (14b): from “She shall touch no sacred thing,” [we learn that it means] eating, and not touching. And this “approaches” is also explained in tractate Me’ila (10b) as meaning not touching but something fit to be brought near [the altar]: Rabbi Elazar said: Is there one who touches and is liable? If so, why is it said “who approaches”? To say that one is not liable for it until it is fit to be offered; that is, one is not liable for eating it in impurity until it is fit to be offered.
rashi:b23.1: Items consecrated for Temple maintenance are excluded: one who eats them while his body is impure is not punished by karet. Here too, then, let all [the forbidden relations] be derived from his sister.
rashi:b25.1: A married woman, who can be permitted in the life of the one who prohibits her: since she can be divorced with a bill of divorce. Therefore she is not derived from his sister, and a sin offering [for each one] within a single lapse is not found with her.
rashi:b26.1: By herself: even if he committed it together with the others.
rashi:b27.1: To judge it with karet and not with lashes: and it would teach about the entire generalization; for he does not hold [the mishna’s principle] that those liable to karet who were flogged are exempt from their karet, in the chapter “These Are the Ones Who Are Flogged” (Makkot 23a).
rashi:b28.1: “And to a woman”: it should have written, “And to a menstruating woman you shall not approach.”
rashi:b29.1: And the Rabbis: who hold that [those liable to karet who were flogged] are exempt from their karet, and who take the karet stated with his sister to separate.
rashi:b29.2: Let them derive it from “And to a woman”: to separate.
rashi:b29.3: For his sister, and for his father’s sister, and for his mother’s sister: for it might have entered your mind that since a single prohibition, that of sisterhood, applies to all of them, he is liable only once.
rashi:b30.1: Aren’t they separate names: this is already derived from “And to a woman.” They are separate verses, since his sister, his father’s sister and his mother’s sister are derived from three verses.
rashi:b30.2: His sister who is his father’s sister and his mother’s sister: this is explained below in the chapter “They Said to Him” (Keritot 15a), with a wicked man son of a wicked man [the Hebrew adds in parentheses: “a Kuti”] who had intercourse with his mother and fathered two daughters, then had intercourse with one of them and fathered a son, and the son had intercourse with his sister [the other daughter], who is his father’s sister and his mother’s sister. For this a verse is needed to separate, since it is one body.
rashi:b32.1: From “his sister” in the latter clause: since the verse of karet above also refers to it.
tosafot:b4.1: To exclude the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov: below in chapter 2 (8b) the Gemara says that the Rabbis did not list the convert because when a convert brings his offering, he brings it in order to enter the congregation. Evidently, according to the Rabbis too a convert lacks atonement; and “to exclude” here means only that the mishna does not deal with that case. Similarly at the beginning of Bava Kamma, and below, the mishna’s tally serves to exclude the lists of Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Ḥiyya.
tosafot:b14.1: Because it teaches in the latter clause, “And a king is like them”: this is not the latter clause of the mishna of “Five bring,” but is taught in Horayot (8b).
tosafot:b16.1: To exclude one who renders piggul: Rashi explained that he does not pay from the best [land]. However, the first chapter of Bava Kamma implies that it excludes him not with regard to paying from the best, but that it does not list him because it does not deal with consecrated items. And the reason the Gemara does not bring here [other tallies, such as] “Fifteen women exempt [their rivals]” and “A woman is acquired in three ways,” and so on, is that those come to exclude the views of amora’im, while here [the tallies] exclude the views of tanna’im. As for “Four new years,” it means four new years differing in their laws from one another; and so too with many [other tallies].
tosafot:b25.1: Who cannot be permitted in the life of the one who prohibits her; a married woman is excluded: he could also have said: just as his sister can never be permitted at all, so too every [relation that can never be permitted], which excludes a brother’s wife, who is permitted where there is a mitzva [of levirate marriage].
tosafot:b26.1: All the forbidden relations are juxtaposed to his sister, of whom karet is written: one cannot ask: let the verse omit the juxtaposition and write karet with a married woman, which is lenient, or with a brother’s wife, and all the more so would it apply to the other relations. For one can answer that this juxtaposition is needed for many matters in Yevamot. Furthermore, [a derivation from them could be refuted]: what of those, which have the feature that it is in his power to increase [them]?
tosafot:b27.1: To judge it with karet and not with lashes: this is puzzling, for with peace offerings too, let us say they were singled out to judge it with karet and not with lashes.
tosafot:b30.1: His sister who is his father’s sister, and so on: it is puzzling that the Gemara chose these, which can come about only through a transgression. Let it choose his brother’s wife who is also his father’s brother’s wife, or his daughter’s daughter who is also his daughter-in-law, and his wife’s sister, as we say in chapter 3 (below, 14a). One can answer that it chose this case for its novelty: although all its names are names of sisterhood, they still count as separate names.
gershom:b1.1: Why do I need the tally, that it teaches thirty-six? Let it say: For these one is liable to karet for their intentional violation: one who has intercourse with a mother, and so on.
gershom:b2.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: That is why it teaches their tally: to say that if he did them all in one lapse of awareness, in one unwitting error, he is liable to thirty-six sin offerings. For had it not stated the tally, one might say there are more of them and it taught some and left others out; or one might have thought that there are some acts for whose intentional violation one is not liable to karet and for whose unwitting violation one is not liable to a sin offering. That is why it teaches the tally: that he is liable for each and every one, and there are no more.
gershom:b3.1: The tally of the primary categories of labor: why do I need it? Let it say: These are the primary categories of labor: sowing and reaping, and so on.
gershom:b4.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan said, and so on: the same reason as for the karet transgressions.
gershom:b5.1: Furthermore, that which we learned in our next chapter: Four lack atonement: the zav, the zava, and so on, who are not permitted teruma and sacrificial food until they bring their atonement offering. The tally comes to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer [ben Ya’akov in the Gemara], who teaches in the Tosefta that a convert lacks atonement: when he has converted, been circumcised and immersed, he still may not eat sacrificial food or enter the congregation until the blood, the blood of bird offerings, is sprinkled on his behalf, as is explained in our second chapter: “And if a stranger sojourns with you, or whoever is among you throughout your generations, and will offer an offering made by fire, of a pleasing aroma to the Lord, as you do, so he shall do” (Numbers 15:14): just as you [bring offerings of] kinds of blood, so they [bring] kinds of blood. Just as your ancestors entered the covenant only through circumcision, immersion and the sprinkling of blood, so they enter the covenant only through circumcision, immersion and the sprinkling of blood. If so, just as your ancestors [brought] a burnt offering and peace offerings, so too converts? You must say: go and see which kind of blood offering is entirely for the fire and has nothing more lenient than it: say this is the bird burnt offering; to bring a single bird. (A printer’s gloss: it seems something is missing here; read: to bring a single bird is impossible; that is, he brings, and so on, in the evening, but in any case he must bring the second; see the passage there.) That is, he brings one bird in the morning and eats sacrificial food in the evening. Had it said “These lack atonement” without saying “four,” I would have said it taught some and left others out, to include this case of Rabbi Eliezer as well. It teaches us “four” and no more, to exclude this case of Rabbi Eliezer.
gershom:b6.1: Furthermore, that which we learned in our second chapter: Four bring an offering for the intentional as for the unwitting: one who has intercourse with the maidservant, a nazirite who became impure, [one who swears] the oath of testimony and the oath on a deposit. And it explains there from where we know that they bring an offering for the intentional as for the unwitting.
gershom:b7.1: Why do I need the tally? To exclude the opinion of Rabbi Shimon, who teaches in tractate Shevuot that the intentional violation of the oath on a deposit was not given atonement. Had it said “These lack atonement” [so in the text; the mishna here is of those who bring for the intentional as for the unwitting] without stating a tally, I would have said it is not precise, but follows Rabbi Shimon, who excludes the oath on a deposit. The tally teaches us that there are four, and excludes Rabbi Shimon’s view.
gershom:b8.1: Furthermore, that which we also learned in our second chapter: Five bring one offering for many transgressions: one who has intercourse with the maidservant many times, and a nazirite who became impure with many impurities, and so on. Why do I need the tally? Because it teaches there: and a nazirite who became impure with many impurities brings only one offering.
gershom:b9.1: And you find it, for example, where he became impure on the seventh and again became impure on the seventh: that is, he became impure with many impurities on the seventh day, the day of his shaving, as it is written: “And if any man dies very suddenly beside him, and he defiles his consecrated head, then he shall shave his head on the day of his cleansing; on the seventh day shall he shave it” (Numbers 6:9). That is the naziriteship of impurity; and it is written: “But the former days shall be void, because his naziriteship was defiled” (Numbers 6:12).
gershom:b10.1: [It takes effect from the seventh day,] and he begins again to count a naziriteship of purity, thirty days. The tally of the mishna, which teaches five and includes among them a nazirite who became impure with many impurities, tells us that it follows Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, who says in tractate Nazir that the naziriteship of purity, which he begins counting again, takes effect on him from the seventh day. Since he became impure on the seventh and again on the seventh, these are many impurities after he began to count the naziriteship of purity; and this impure nazirite had not yet reached the eighth day, the time fit for bringing an offering, for that is not until the eighth day, as it is written: “And on the eighth day he shall take two unblemished lambs” [the wording of Leviticus 14:10].
gershom:b11.1: For if you say it is Rabbi: the mishna. Since Rabbi says that the naziriteship of purity does not take effect on him until the eighth, when it is fit to bring an offering, then according to Rabbi, where do you find that he became impure with many impurities and brings only one offering?
gershom:b12.1: If he became impure on the seventh, and again on the seventh, and again on the seventh: since according to Rabbi the naziriteship of purity has not yet taken effect on him, all these impurities are, for Rabbi, one long impurity, like the first single impurity, and they are not many impurities.
gershom:b13.1: And if he became impure on the eighth, and again on the eighth, and again on the eighth: since according to Rabbi the naziriteship of purity has already taken effect on him, for he went out at a time fit for bringing an offering on the eighth, and afterward became impure with many impurities, he is liable to an offering for each and every one.
gershom:b14.1: Rather, conclude from the tally of the mishna, which teaches five and includes a nazirite who became impure with many impurities, that it is Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, and it excludes Rabbi’s view. Although elsewhere we say the halakha follows Rabbi against his colleague, it teaches us that here it does not.
gershom:b15.1: As it is taught: “And he shall sanctify his head that same day”: that is, he begins to count his naziriteship of purity. And when? Rabbi holds that “that same day” is the day of bringing the offering, that is, the eighth day.
gershom:b16.1: And Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says: it speaks of the day of his shaving, that is, the seventh day.
gershom:b17.1: Furthermore, that which we also learned in our second chapter: Five bring a sliding-scale offering: for the hearing of the voice, for the utterance of the lips, for defiling the Temple and its sacred foods, and the woman after childbirth, and the leper.
gershom:b18.1: Why do I need the tally of five?
gershom:b19.1: Because it teaches in the latter clause of that mishna of Horayot: The court is not liable for the hearing of the voice, for the utterance of the lips, or for defiling the Temple and its sacred foods; and the king is liable for all of them, as are an individual and the anointed priest, who are liable for all of them; this is the statement of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili. Rabbi Akiva says: The king is liable for all of them except the hearing of the voice of the oath, since the king, that is, the nasi, neither testifies nor is testified against.
gershom:b20.1: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds: whoever is subject to one of them is subject to all of them. The mishna that teaches five tells us that it follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva, and excludes Rabbi Eliezer, who says there in Horayot that a king brings a goat. The tally tells us: five bring a sliding-scale offering, even a king.
gershom:b21.1: Why do I need the tally? To exclude Rabbi Oshaya, who says there are thirteen primary categories of damage: the unpaid bailee, the borrower, and so on. Had it said, “These are the primary categories of damage: the ox and the pit,” I would have said it taught some and left out those of Rabbi Oshaya. It tells us “four primary categories,” to exclude Rabbi Oshaya’s. What is the reason? For Rav according to his view, and for Shmuel according to his. According to Rav, who says maveh is a person, it excludes Rabbi Oshaya’s because the tanna taught “person” and everything resembling it. According to Shmuel, who says maveh is the tooth, he would tell you that the tanna deals with damage done by one’s property and not by one’s body, to exclude Rabbi Oshaya’s, which are damage done by the body.
gershom:b22.1: And according to Rabbi Oshaya, who teaches thirteen, why do I need the tally? To exclude Rabbi Ḥiyya, who says there are twenty-four primary categories of damage. And why does Rabbi Oshaya exclude them? Because he holds that he deals with [ordinary] payment and not with fines, and those of Rabbi Ḥiyya are fines.
gershom:b23.1: And according to Rabbi Ḥiyya, why do I need his tally? To exclude one who renders consecrated offerings piggul: a priest who says, “I am slaughtering so-and-so’s offering on condition of burning an olive-bulk of it beyond its time”; and the informer, who informs on his fellow’s money to gentile oppressors. These are exempt from payment, since they do not act with their hands but by mere speech. And if it is difficult for Rabbi Ḥiyya: if so, conspiring witnesses and a defamer, whom he does count, also act by mere speech! He would answer you: of conspiring witnesses an act is written, as it is written, “as he had schemed to do” (Deuteronomy 19:19); and of the defamer it says that he performed an act, since he said, “I did not find your daughter a virgin” (Deuteronomy 22:17). Therefore he counts them.
gershom:b24.1: Granted, you cannot find that he is entirely exempt from a sin offering, since karet is written for all of them, which means that for their unwitting violation there is a sin offering.
gershom:b25.1: That is why karet was singled out with his sister: to separate, to make him liable for each and every one. Just as his sister is distinct in that she is a forbidden relation, for whose intentional violation one is liable to karet and for whose unwitting violation one is liable to a sin offering, so too every forbidden relation: one is liable to karet for its intentional violation and to a sin offering for its unwitting violation.
gershom:b26.1: But weren’t peace offerings included in [the category of] all sacrificial offerings? As it is written: “Say to them: Throughout your generations, any man of all your seed who approaches the sacred things …” (Leviticus 22:3). So too his sister was singled out of the generalization to teach about the entire generalization.
gershom:b27.1: Rav Beivai would tell you: “And from it” [Rabbeinu Gershom reads umina, “and from it,” where the printed Gemara reads bar mina, “apart from it”]: for the baraita itself supports him: didn’t you say, and so on.
gershom:b28.1: Here too: just as his sister is distinct in that she is a forbidden relation who can never be permitted in the life of the one who prohibits her, since she is never permitted to her brother who prohibits her, so too for every [relation] who cannot be permitted in the life of the one who prohibits her, one is liable to karet.
gershom:b29.1: Excluding a married woman, who can be permitted in the life of the one who prohibits her, since if he gave her a bill of divorce she is permitted; and likewise a menstruating woman is permitted to her husband after her menstruation. Therefore his sister cannot teach about the entire generalization.
gershom:b30.1: Rabbi Yona said, and so on: from here you derive [the rule] to separate, for the verse states: “For whoever shall do any of these abominations …” (Leviticus 18:29), and all the forbidden relations, whether his sister, a married woman or a menstruating woman, belong to this verse. Since that is so, since his sister belongs to this verse and was singled out, conclude from it that this is a juxtaposition, and one does not refute a juxtaposition. Rather, just as for this one that was singled out one is liable for her by herself, so too for all the others, even those who can be permitted in the life of the one who prohibits them.
gershom:b31.1: And according to Rabbi Yitzḥak, who disagrees in tractate Makkot with what we learned there, “All those liable to karet who were flogged are exempt from their karet,” and who takes (a printer’s gloss: read “takes this”) the karet written with his sister, which was singled out to judge them, and so on: why was karet singled out with his sister? To judge them with karet and not with lashes. If so, from where does he derive [the rule] to separate, to make him liable for each one?
gershom:b32.1: He derives it from “And to a woman in the impurity of her menstruation”: since it could have said, “And to a menstruating woman in her impurity,” why does it say “And to a woman”? Conclude from it: to separate for each and every woman among the forbidden relations, since this “And to a woman” is adjacent to the passage of the forbidden relations.
gershom:b33.1: They need it to separate, to make him liable for his sister, for his father’s sister and for his mother’s sister.
gershom:b34.1: Why do they need these to separate? It is obvious that he is liable for each one by itself, since the names are separate, this one being called his sister, this one his father’s sister and this one his mother’s sister, and the bodies are separate, since they are three women.
gershom:b35.1: Rather, say: they need it to separate for his sister who is his father’s sister and who is his mother’s sister. You find it with a wicked man son of a wicked man: for example, one who had intercourse with his mother and fathered two daughters by her, then had intercourse with one of the daughters and fathered a son, and that son had intercourse with the other daughter, who is his sister through his father, his mother’s sister and his father’s sister. Here the names are separate but the body is one. They need it to make him liable for his sister who is both his father’s daughter and his mother’s daughter, since in the verse we find only “your father’s daughter or your mother’s daughter” [Leviticus 18:9]. (A printer’s mark notes that the text up to here belongs to the previous page.) [This continues the Gemara on 3a:] to say that one does not punish on the basis of an inference, even though it would follow by a fortiori reasoning: if for his father’s daughter who is not his mother’s daughter he is liable, then for his father’s daughter who is also his mother’s daughter, all the more so.
gershom:b36.1: [On the Gemara’s continuation on 3a:] And Rabbi Yitzḥak does not need a verse for this, since he holds that one does punish on the basis of an inference.
gershom:b37.1: [On the Gemara’s continuation on 3a:] And if you wish, say: above he responds to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said that karet was singled out with his sister to separate. If you wish, say: [as for the rule] to separate, he derives the punishment from the warning: just as the warning, that is, the prohibition, is written for each and every forbidden relation, so too the punishment of karet [is as if written for each of them], and he is liable for each and every forbidden relation.
